#### Sermon Outline From Dave

# The Cross, Substitution, and the True Elder Brother

## The idea of substitution

It is a deeply human impulse to want someone else to absorb the consequence or debt that we owe. The Christian understanding of the cross centers on the truth that **someone else actually did**—Jesus willingly took the penalty for our sin and bore what we could not.

A key New Testament phrase is **“hyper hemon”** (Greek: *for us*), which expresses the idea of substitution: something being done **on our behalf**, in our place, for our sake.  
- In **Romans 5:7–8**, Paul writes:  
  > Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though perhaps for a good person someone might even dare to die. But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.  
  [Romans 5:7–8 (Bible Gateway)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans+5%3A7-8&version=NIV)  

- In **1 John 3:16**, the idea appears again:  
  > This is how we know what love is: Jesus Christ laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters.  

- In **1 Corinthians 15:3**, Paul defines the gospel as:  
  > For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.  

- In **John 10:11**, Jesus says,  
  > I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.  

- The pattern is clear: the cross is not merely a backdrop to ethics; it is a **substitutionary event** in which Jesus willingly, sacrificially took our place.

## The story of the two sons and the father (Luke 15:11–32)

Jesus explains the cross not with a theological lecture, but with a story—a family story about **two sons, a father, and a broken relationship**.  
- In **Luke 15:11–32**, Jesus tells of a man with two sons. The younger son demands his inheritance early, effectively saying, “I wish you were dead so I can have your money now.”  
- The father gives him his share, the younger son leaves for a distant country, and squanders everything in reckless, “wild living,” becoming destitute and feeding pigs—a shockingly shameful state for a Jew.  
- When he comes to his senses (“rock bottom”), he plans to return home and say,  
  > “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.”  
  [Luke 15:11–32 (Bible Gateway)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+15%3A11-32&version=NIV)  

- But the father does not wait for the speech. When he sees his son coming from a distance, he runs to him, embraces him, restores his status with a robe and ring, and throws a great feast.

## The older brother and the cost of the welcome

The story takes a sharp turn with the introduction of the **older brother**.  
- The older brother hears the music and learns that the party is for his younger brother, who has squandered the father’s property.  
- Luke 15:28–30 records his anger:  
  > The older brother became angry and refused to go in. So his father went out and pleaded with him. But he answered his father, “Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”  
- In the cultural setting, when the father divided the estate the older brother would receive **two‑thirds** and the younger **one‑third**. That means the celebration is paid for largely from the older brother’s share.  
- The younger son’s welcome home is **free for him**, but **not free overall**: someone still has to bear the cost. The older brother refuses to absorb that cost and therefore refuses to go in.

## The cross is not just an example

The story shows that the cross is more than **inspiration** (“Jesus died to show us how loving we should be”); it is **rescue**.  
- The younger son represents anyone who has wandered far from God, morally bankrupt and spiritually destitute.  
- The father represents God, whose instinct is **compassion and restoration**, not rejection.  
- The older brother represents those who feel they have “earned” their place and are unwilling to let the cost be born on their behalf—or to extend grace to others.  
- The real problem is not just distance from God, but the truth that **we cannot repair ourselves**. The Bible describes humanity as **enslaved to sin**, trapped under death, and spiritually dead apart from Christ (see, for example, Romans 6; Hebrews 2; Ephesians 2).

## The older brother’s refusal and the unanswered question

Jesus leaves the story unresolved:  
- The older brother stands outside, the father is pleading with him, and the question hangs in the air: **If the older brother will not pay the cost, who will**?  
- The older brother does not just refuse out of pride; there is also an underlying **inability**. The New Testament often speaks of sin as a **debt** so great that we cannot pay it.  
- The implication is that even if the older brother wanted to, he could not cover the cost that the younger brother owes. The debt is **insurmountable**.

## Jesus as the true elder brother

In this light, New Testament writers point to **Jesus** as the one who actually plays the role of the **true elder brother**.

- In **Romans 8:29**, Paul writes:  
  > For those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.  
  [Romans 8:29 (Bible Gateway)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans+8%3A29&version=NIV)  

- In **Hebrews 2:11–13**, the author says:  
  > Both the one who makes people holy and those who are made holy are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters. He says, “I will declare your name to my brothers and sisters; in the assembly I will sing your praises.”  
  [Hebrews 2:11–13 (Bible Gateway)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hebrews+2%3A11-13&version=NIV)  

These passages reveal that:

- Jesus is the **true elder brother** who willingly bears the cost that we could not.  
- He is **not ashamed** to call us brothers and sisters.  
- He leaves everything to come looking for us, absorbs the debt, and brings us home.

## What happened on the cross

Across the New Testament, the cross is described as a **historical, substitutionary event**:

- **Christ bore our sins** in His body on the cross (1 Peter 2:24).  
- **Christ became a curse for us**, redeeming us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13).  
- **Christ died for the ungodly** while we were still sinners (Romans 5:6–8). [Romans 5:7–8 (Bible Gateway)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans+5%3A7-8&version=NIV)  
- **John 3:16** captures the motive behind it all:  
  > For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.  
  [John 3:16 (Bible Gateway)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+3%3A16&version=NIV)  

Paul also draws the logical conclusion in **Romans 8:31–32**:  
- If God is for us, who can be against us?  
- He who did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, will He not also graciously give us all things?  
  [Romans 8:31–32 (Bible Gateway)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans+8%3A31-32&version=NIV)  

Substitution is therefore a **real transaction**—a real payment that we could not make—but it is motivated by **love**, with the purpose of bringing us home.

## The call to “come home”

The story and the New Testament together point to a simple but profound invitation: **Come home**.

- The older brother had the opportunity to join the party, to share in the celebration, but he stayed outside because of resentment and refusal to absorb the cost.  
- The father represents God saying, “Everything I have is yours. We had to celebrate because this son was lost and is now found.”  
- The true elder brother, Jesus, steps in not only to **pay the cost**, but to **invite others in**:  
  - Those who feel far from God.  
  - Those who feel trapped under shame and brokenness.  
  - Those who think they have gone too far to be welcome.  

Implicit in the text is both a **personal response** and a **missional response**:

- **Personally**, you are invited to come home to the Father, not based on your performance, but on the substitutionary work of the true elder brother.  
- **Relationally**, you are invited to extend the same invitation to others: to pray for them, to speak words of “come home,” and to invite them into the celebration of grace.

## The shape of a life under substitution

A life that understands substitution looks like this:

- It knows that **salvation is not self‑achievement**; it is rescue.  
- It is marked by **gratitude**, not pride, because the cost was paid by another.  
- It is willing, like the true elder brother, to **bear cost for others**, to help bring the “lost” home.  
- It worships the Father who sent the Son and the Son who willingly gave Himself, knowing that if substitution is true, then **God’s heart toward us is radically different** from what we fear it to be.

In short, substitution is not a cold, mechanical transaction; it is **the Father’s love**, expressed through the **Son’s obedience**, bringing **prodigal sons and resentful older brothers** alike into the same family, at the same table, with the same invitation: **Come home**.
